--- title: "Training, validation and test data" description: "Why you hold data back, what each held-back piece is for, and why a random split is the wrong split for a marine survey." order: 6 categories: [data-preparation, validation] --- ## The one honest measurement [Section 1](../01-introduction/what-is-machine-learning.qmd) compared a straight line with a decision tree on stations that neither model had seen during fitting. A model's own output cannot show how well it predicts new stations. Only data the model has never seen can. That is the entire function of a held-back set: it is the only honest measurement you have. Everything in this page is about protecting it, and in marine data, protecting it takes more than a random split. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. The R tab is what produced the tables and figures you see; the Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent, shown for translation rather than executed by the site. Figures stay in R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. It is real code, not pseudocode: it runs against the same files through `python/mlbasic_data.py`, and `python/check-snippets.py` executes every snippet in the site to keep it honest. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly**: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea ### Three roles, not three files - **Training data**: the model learns its parameters from this. Coefficients, split points, weights. - **Validation data**: used to *choose*: which model, which hyperparameters, which features. Choosing is a form of learning, so these choices must not be made on the test set. - **Test data**: used once, at the end, to report how well the chosen model does. Look at it twice and it stops being a test set. The middle role is the one people skip, and skipping it is how results get oversold. If you try eight models and report the best one's test score, that score is the maximum of eight noisy numbers, which is biased upward, and the more things you try, the worse it gets. The test set answers *how good is this model*, never *which model is best*. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The place of cross-validation A separate validation set is wasteful when data is scarce, which in marine science is always. Cross-validation replaces it: split the training data into folds, and let each fold take a turn as the validation set. The test set is untouched and still used once. [Section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) covers this properly; for now, note that cross-validation is a smarter way to do validation, not a replacement for holding out a test set. ::: ### The size of the test set Common splits are 70/30, 75/25 and 80/20. There is no principle behind the specific numbers: it is a trade-off between training the model well and measuring it precisely. With a few hundred rows, a 25% test set is small enough that its score is noisy; with hundreds of thousands, 5% is plenty. What matters far more is *how* you split. ### Stratify when a class is rare A random split of a 5% class can easily leave you with a test set containing barely any of it. `strata =` makes the split preserve the proportion in both halves. ### The marine problem: random is not the same as independent A random split assumes rows are interchangeable. Marine data's rows are not, for the reasons in [the first page of this section](observations-and-features.qmd): repeat visits to a site, spatial proximity, and time. If station A and station B are two visits to the same site, and A lands in training while B lands in test, the model has effectively seen B. Its test score measures how well it memorised a site, not how well it generalises to a new one, and the score will be high. ## Worked example ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_raw() |> distinct() |> mutate( salinity_psu = na_if(salinity_psu, -999), temperature_c = na_if(temperature_c, -999), depth_m = if_else(depth_m > 250, depth_m / 10, depth_m), substrate = factor(str_to_lower(str_trim(substrate))), substrate = fct_collapse(substrate, sand = c("sand", "sandy"), mud = c("mud", "muddy"), gravel = "gravel", rock = c("rock", "rocky")), rare_species = factor(rare_species, levels = c("yes", "no")) ) nrow(survey) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 800 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit, train_test_split from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean # The same cleaning as the R tab, kept in python/mlbasic_data.py so it does not # have to be repeated on every page. survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() len(survey) ``` ::: ### A plain random split ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plain <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75) tibble(training = nrow(training(plain)), testing = nrow(testing(plain))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| training| testing| |--------:|-------:| | 600| 200|
::: ::: ## Python ```python plain_train, plain_test = train_test_split(survey, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) pd.DataFrame({"training": [len(plain_train)], "testing": [len(plain_test)]}) ``` ::: ### Stratifying on a rare class Our rare species is present at 5% of stations. Ask for a stratified split: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) unstratified <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75) stratified <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75, strata = rare_species) bind_rows( tibble(split = "Unstratified", train_pct = 100 * mean(training(unstratified)$rare_species == "yes"), test_pct = 100 * mean(testing(unstratified)$rare_species == "yes")), tibble(split = "Stratified (as asked)", train_pct = 100 * mean(training(stratified)$rare_species == "yes"), test_pct = 100 * mean(testing(stratified)$rare_species == "yes")) ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|split | train_pct| test_pct| |:---------------------|---------:|--------:| |Unstratified | 4.67| 6.5| |Stratified (as asked) | 6.00| 2.5|
::: ::: ## Python ```python unstrat_train, unstrat_test = train_test_split( survey, train_size=0.75, random_state=2026) strat_train, strat_test = train_test_split( survey, train_size=0.75, random_state=2026, stratify=survey["rare_species"]) def prevalence(frame): return round(100 * (frame["rare_species"] == "yes").mean(), 2) pd.DataFrame([ {"split": "Unstratified", "train_pct": prevalence(unstrat_train), "test_pct": prevalence(unstrat_test)}, {"split": "Stratified (as asked)", "train_pct": prevalence(strat_train), "test_pct": prevalence(strat_test)}, ]) ``` ::: Look at that carefully. The species is present at 5.1% of all stations, and the *stratified* split produced 6.0% in training against 2.5% in test. Stratification does not do that. It did not happen. ::: {.callout-warning} ## `strata` can be ignored without telling you `rsample` pools strata that are smaller than the `pool` argument, which defaults to `0.1`. Our rare class is 5.1% of the data, below the threshold, so it was pooled away and the split fell back to unstratified. Silently: no error, and on this version no warning either. This is the quietest failure in the whole section. You asked for the safety measure, the code ran, and you did not get it. scikit-learn has no pooling step, so `stratify=` splits the rare class directly and the Python tab holds the prevalence from the start. That is a difference in defaults, not a difference in principle: the lesson below applies to whichever you use. ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) properly <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75, strata = rare_species, pool = 0.01) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: Stratifying groups that make up 1% of the data may be statistically risky. #> ℹ Consider increasing `pool` to at least 0.1. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tibble( train_pct = round(100 * mean(training(properly)$rare_species == "yes"), 2), test_pct = round(100 * mean(testing(properly)$rare_species == "yes"), 2) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| train_pct| test_pct| |---------:|--------:| | 5.01| 5.47|
::: ::: ## Python ```python # scikit-learn's stratify has no pooling step to opt out of: it splits each # class directly, so the rare class is already divided as closely as the counts # allow. The R tab needs pool = 0.01 to get the same behaviour. pd.DataFrame({ "train_pct": [prevalence(strat_train)], "test_pct": [prevalence(strat_test)], }) ``` ::: Now it holds: 5.0% against 5.5%, either side of the 5.1% in the full data. Note that lowering `pool` produces a warning of its own, and the warning is fair: stratifying on 41 positive cases is statistically thin. But thin and honest beats absent and silent. The general lesson is bigger than one argument: **check that a safeguard did what you asked**, by looking at the result rather than at the code. ### The split that respects sites ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grouped <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train_g <- training(grouped) test_g <- testing(grouped) tibble( training_rows = nrow(train_g), testing_rows = nrow(test_g), sites_in_both = length(intersect(train_g$site_id, test_g$site_id)) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| training_rows| testing_rows| sites_in_both| |-------------:|------------:|-------------:| | 602| 198| 0|
::: ::: ## Python ```python grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train_g, test_g = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] pd.DataFrame({ "training_rows": [len(train_g)], "testing_rows": [len(test_g)], "sites_in_both": [len(set(train_g["site_id"]) & set(test_g["site_id"]))], }) ``` ::: No site appears in both halves. Compare that with the random split: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble( `random split: sites in both halves` = length(intersect(training(plain)$site_id, testing(plain)$site_id)), `random split: test rows at a site the model has seen` = sum(testing(plain)$site_id %in% training(plain)$site_id), `as a percentage of the test set` = round(100 * mean(testing(plain)$site_id %in% training(plain)$site_id), 1) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| random split: sites in both halves| random split: test rows at a site the model has seen| as a percentage of the test set| |----------------------------------:|----------------------------------------------------:|-------------------------------:| | 120| 200| 100|
::: ::: ## Python ```python seen = plain_test["site_id"].isin(plain_train["site_id"]) pd.DataFrame({ "random split: sites in both halves": [len(set(plain_train["site_id"]) & set(plain_test["site_id"]))], "random split: test rows at a site the model has seen": [int(seen.sum())], "as a percentage of the test set": [round(100 * seen.mean(), 1)], }) ``` ::: Under the random split, *every single one* of the 200 test stations sits at a site the model has already trained on. Not most, all of them. Whatever that test set is measuring, it is not performance at a new location, which is what a habitat map is for. ## Two splits, two questions Two splits of the same data, two different questions: | Split | Question it answers | | --- | --- | | Random | How well does the model predict *another station at a site I have surveyed*? | | Grouped by site | How well does the model predict *a site I have never surveyed*? | Both are legitimate. They are not interchangeable, and the second is usually what marine work claims and the first is usually what marine work measures. The gap between the two numbers is the size of that mistake, and [section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) measures it directly. The rule that follows is short: **split along whatever dimension you intend to generalise across.** New sites, split by site. Next year, split by year. A new survey vessel, split by vessel. If you will only ever predict more stations within the same programme, a random split is honest. ## Limits of a single split **The test set is a single draw.** With 200 test rows, its score carries real uncertainty, and two different seeds give two different answers. Report it as an estimate, not a measurement. **Splitting by group shrinks the effective size of both halves.** 160 sites split 75/25 gives 120 training sites and 40 test sites, and 40 is not many. Honest and small beats optimistic and large, but the cost is real. **Hold-out sets erode with use.** Every time you check the test set and change something, a little of its independence is spent. The only defence is discipline: decide everything on the training data, then look once. **Stratifying on a continuous outcome is possible but blunt.** `strata =` bins the variable first, which is fine for a skewed response and not a substitute for thinking about what makes your data unbalanced. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Training fits, validation chooses, test reports. Using the test set to choose turns it into a validation set and inflates your result. - Stratify when a class is rare, or your test set may contain too few of it to measure anything. - A random split assumes rows are interchangeable. Repeat visits, spatial proximity and time all break that assumption. - Split along the dimension you intend to generalise across: new sites, new years, new vessels. - Here, a random split puts most test stations at sites the model has already trained on, so it answers a much easier question than the one being asked. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Run the random split with three different seeds and record the proportion of the rare species in each test set. How much does it move? 2. Fit the same model under `initial_split()` and under `group_initial_split()`, and compare test RMSE. The difference is what a random split was hiding, and it is the subject of [section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd).
